title: Why Healthcare Is a Strong Opportunity for UCaaS Vendors
summary: Healthcare is a fast-growing UCaaS vertical. Discover buyer needs, partner opportunities, and how to position your portfolio for growth.
body_markdown:
A medical group asks you for a quote to replace its phone system. But a few questions into the conversation, you discover that patients struggle to reach the scheduling team and a recently acquired clinic is still running on a separate system.


Now you’re looking at a potentially much bigger deal.


Healthcare offers UCaaS resellers plenty of opportunities like this. The challenge is knowing what to look for, how to sell into a regulated industry, and which services can help you grow the account over time. Let’s look at where the opportunities are, what healthcare buyers expect, and how Sangoma can help you win their business.


# The Market Case for Unified Communications in Healthcare


According to Mordor Intelligence,[the global healthcare UCaaS market is estimated at $5.83 billion in 2026](https://www.mordorintelligence.com/industry-reports/unified-communications-as-a-service-in-healthcare) , with forecasts putting it at $10.11 billion by 2031. That represents a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 11.62%.


The demand makes sense when you look at how healthcare providers operate. Video consultations need reliable connections. Integrating communications with electronic health records (EHRs) can save staff from entering the same information twice. And with value-based care placing greater emphasis on patient outcomes, keeping in touch with patients and coordinating care between visits has become a bigger part of the job.


For resellers, there’s a good case for developing a healthcare-specific sales approach. But healthcare is a broad market. A small independent practice has very different needs from a physician group running twenty clinics. Pick a segment and learn how its teams communicate and where challenges typically arise. Then build your demos, security documentation and implementation plans around the problems those customers actually deal with.


# What Makes Healthcare Buyers Different from Other Verticals


Healthcare buyers need to understand how a proposed system will affect patient access and the handling of sensitive information. Their questions extend to clinical workflows, individual locations and who takes responsibility when a service fails.


## Compliance Is the Main Qualification Factor


For US healthcare organizations subject to HIPAA, compliance is a qualification requirement. A vendor’s claim of HIPAA support still needs to be backed by an explanation of the services covered, their configuration and each party’s involvement.


[HHS guidance on cloud computing](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/health-information-technology/cloud-computing/index.html) explains that a cloud provider creating, receiving, maintaining or transmitting electronic protected health information on a covered entity’s behalf is generally a business associate. A business associate agreement (BAA) is required for that relationship. A narrow exception applies to transmission-only conduits.


Buyers need answers to questions such as:


- Which quoted services are covered by the BAA, including recording, transcription and third-party AI processing?
- Who can access recordings and transcripts, and how are retention and deletion managed?
- How are voice, video and stored files protected, including encryption?
- What audit logs are available for messaging, file access and administrative changes?


A signed BAA is one part of compliance. The provider and its vendors still need appropriate safeguards and risk management. Documenting data flows and controls helps a partner explain how features that handle patient information fit those requirements.


## Multi-Site and Multi-Location Complexity


A physician group may need one communications system across a main clinic, satellite offices and an imaging center. Each location has its own numbers, opening hours and routing requirements, while the IT team needs central oversight.


Show buyers how the system would work across their locations. For example, demonstrate how to update a clinic’s holiday greeting, redirect overflow calls to another site, or manage users across several clinics from one place. Don’t overlook business continuity. What happens if a clinic loses power or internet connectivity? Which services keep working, and how can patients still reach staff?


[Multi-site projects](https://sangoma.com/blog/integrated-communications-multi-location-reliability/) can also bring partners additional deployment work and ongoing support revenue. The proposal should spell out who will handle number porting, arrange backup connectivity and test call routing at each location.


## EHR Integration Can Be a Critical Buying Factor


EHR connectivity can be a deciding factor when healthcare organizations need[communications integrated into their existing clinical workflows](https://sangoma.com/solutions/healthcare/) . With the right integration, staff can identify a matching patient record when someone calls, pull up their chart and log call details directly in the EHR, without entering the same information twice.


“We have an API” sounds promising until a practice asks to see an appointment booked or a call logged directly in its EHR. Then you need to know exactly what the connector supports for that particular system and software version. Show the buyer what already works, and find out what would require custom development before you promise it in the proposal.


Caller ID also needs careful handling. Shared household numbers and outdated records can produce ambiguous matches; staff must still verify the patient’s identity.


Before quoting an EHR integration, find out how the staff will actually use it. A receptionist may only need to look up a patient when a call comes in. A centralized patient access team might also need to book appointments and log calls directly in the EHR. Check what the system allows, which permissions and licences are required, and how much work it will take to get everything running and keep it working.


## Healthcare Sales Cycles Can Be Longer, but Opportunities Can Be Larger


Healthcare procurement can bring clinical, security, legal, finance and IT teams into the decision. Each team evaluates a different part of the proposal, from patient access to data handling and multi-year costs. Coordinating those reviews takes time, particularly across several locations.


The commercial return depends on the account. A multi-site deployment can bring a larger initial contract and later expansion as the organization adds locations. Once the system is established, a partner who understands the customer’s workflows and delivers reliable support has a useful foundation for renewal.


A great demo won’t get a contract signed if the security team has concerns about call recordings or IT hasn’t approved the EHR integration. Find out what could hold up the deal before committing to a deployment date.


# Where the Revenue Sits for Partners and Resellers


The first phone contract might cover one clinic. Then the group acquires two more, the scheduling team starts drowning in calls, and IT wants help keeping every location connected. These additional needs create opportunities to expand the customer relationship.


Seat subscriptions provide the recurring revenue base. Contact center, connectivity and managed security can add to it, provided you have the resources to deliver and support those services.


### More Clinics, More Seat Revenue


A new clinic, practice acquisition or added specialty means more users to connect. You already know the customer’s system and call flows, so much of the groundwork is done, although new locations may still need budget approval or revised contract terms.


The key is making expansion manageable. Centralized user provisioning, reusable site configurations and phased number porting help as a customer[grows from one location to twenty](https://sangoma.com/blog/how-to-scale-business-phone-system/) . Each site’s hours and call routing still need testing, and licensing, capacity and support must keep up with growth.


### Contact Center


A practice can have a perfectly good phone system and still leave patients stuck on hold. Look at the call data: when are queues busiest, how many calls go unanswered, and which requests need clinical staff rather than the front desk?


Callbacks, skills-based routing and queue reporting can help tackle those problems.[Selling UCaaS and contact center together](https://sangoma.com/blog/why-selling-ucaas-alone-limits-partner-growth/) also gives you a bigger role in managing patient access, with recurring revenue from both services. Just check how the contact center fits existing workflows and systems, especially the privacy requirements around recording and automation.


### Connectivity and Security Turn a Phone Sale Into a Managed Account


When call quality deteriorates, the phone system often gets the blame. But poor voice quality can just as easily be traced back to underlying network issues. That’s a good reason to talk about backup internet connections, firewall management and SD-WAN for sites with multiple links.


[Sangoma’s managed network and connectivity services](https://sangoma.com/products/managed-network-and-connectivity/) let partners support the infrastructure behind cloud calling. Depending on the package, connectivity, monitoring and[managed security](https://sangoma.com/products/managed-security/) can add recurring revenue as customers expand.


Supporting both voice and networking also gives you better visibility when something goes wrong, with fewer providers passing the problem around. By bringing communications, connectivity and security together, partners can simplify service management, improve troubleshooting and give customers a more consistent support experience. Clear escalation procedures remain essential. Reliable service and responsive support are what ultimately drive customer retention.


# Why Healthcare Providers Are Moving Toward UCaaS


An operational change often creates the opening for a communications project. The most useful prospecting signals point to a specific need:


- **Legacy PBX end-of-life** . An approaching support deadline or difficulty finding replacement equipment gives a practice a reason to review its options. The system’s confirmed support status helps establish the timing of the project.
- **Telehealth adoption** . Video care creates new coordination needs between patients, clinicians and administrative staff. Some providers can meet those needs through a broader communications platform; others need to retain a specialist telehealth application.
- **Acquisitions.** Combining practices can leave multiple phone systems, numbering plans and support contracts to reconcile. UCaaS can simplify administration across the group, with migration work shaped by existing devices and local requirements.
- **Staffing shortages.** Callbacks, routing and voicemail transcription can reduce administrative work and help staff handle demand. Automated scheduling requires a working scheduling integration, with a route to clinical staff when a request needs their attention.
- **Patient access problems.**[Unanswered calls and long holds](https://sangoma.com/blog/doctors-losing-patients-over-missed-calls-how-sangomas-healthcare-communications-can-help/) create a measurable reason to review the system. Call abandonment, response times and appointment access give practice managers a baseline for evaluating changes.


Each trigger calls for a different conversation. A newly acquired clinic needs a consolidation plan. A practice with overloaded scheduling lines needs to understand when calls arrive, where they go unanswered and how staff can handle them more effectively.

# Frequently Asked Questions


## How big is the unified communications in healthcare market?


Mordor Intelligence estimates the global healthcare UCaaS market at $5.83 billion in 2026, rising to $10.11 billion by 2031 at an 11.62% CAGR. The estimate covers the UCaaS segment of healthcare communications.


## What compliance requirements do UCaaS vendors need to meet for healthcare?


In the US, vendors acting as business associates must meet applicable HIPAA obligations and enter into a BAA. Buyers also need to assess access controls, data protection, retention and audit capabilities across the proposed services. Requirements differ by jurisdiction and workflow.


## Why is healthcare a better vertical opportunity than general SMB for channel partners?


Healthcare can offer multi-site contracts and demand for contact center, connectivity and managed security services. The opportunity is strongest for partners able to support regulated workflows and more involved procurement. Small practices may have budgets and buying processes similar to other small businesses.


## What integrations matter most when selling UCaaS to healthcare providers?


The buyer’s EHR and scheduling system are the starting point. Patient lookup, call logging and appointment workflows are useful functions to demonstrate for the specific systems in use. Fax and staff collaboration tools may also be part of the requirement.


## Can partners sell hybrid or on-premises UC into healthcare, or is it cloud-only?


Cloud, hybrid and on-premises deployments can all fit healthcare requirements. Availability needs, existing equipment, network conditions and internal policy guide the choice. Every deployment also needs a continuity plan for outages.


## How do I start building a healthcare pipeline as a UCaaS reseller?


Choose a customer segment and look for triggers such as an acquisition, new location or approaching PBX support deadline. Learn its workflows, prepare security documentation and build a relevant demonstration. Confirm the buyer’s EHR and approval process early.
